title: Iran Stands Firm on Hormuz Conditions Following Trump's Rejection
snippet: Tehran remains defiant on its strict demands to reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz after President Donald Trump dismissed Iran's proposed seven-day truce plan.
content:
WASHINGTON — Tehran is refusing to back down from its demands for reopening the vital Strait of Hormuz, maintaining a defiant stance Sunday after President Donald Trump dismissed its latest peace proposal as a sign of weakness.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi recently put forward a "seven-day plan" through Qatari mediators aimed at restoring maritime transit through the strategic energy passage. However, the proposal hinges on steep concessions: an immediate halt to all U.S. and allied military operations in the region, the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets, the removal of oil sanctions, and an end to the U.S. naval blockade.

Trump Administration Shoots Down Proposal

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled," Araghchi declared, according to Iranian state media. "We will not back down from them."

President Trump swiftly rejected the offer over the weekend, asserting that Tehran is attempting to negotiate out of desperation. "They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters. U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz further criticized the plan on NBC News, calling it a "cynical attempt" to secure massive sanction relief just to hold talks.

Simmering Tensions and Regional Impact

Adding to the friction, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Sunday to have captured an unmanned American underwater drone in the Strait of Hormuz, alleging it was conducting espionage. The incident highlights the volatile environment in the waterway, where commercial shipping has faced persistent attacks over the seven-month conflict.

The stalemate has drawn sharp concern from regional powers. At the United Nations, Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan condemned the disruption of international shipping lanes, criticizing the international community for failing to protect global energy supplies. Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, reiterating that while Iran remains open to diplomacy, Tehran "no longer trusts the United States."
